chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Bald Hills, Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky's estate, lay forty miles east of Smolensk and two miles from the main road to Moscow.

That same evening the prince gave his instructions to Alpatych, Dessalles asked to see Princess Mary and told her that, since the prince was not well and was taking no steps to ensure his safety, and since Prince Andrew's letter made it clear that staying at Bald Hills might be dangerous, he respectfully advised her to send a letter with Alpatych to the Provincial Governor at Smolensk, asking about the state of affairs and the extent of the danger to Bald Hills. Dessalles wrote this letter for Princess Mary, she signed it, and it was given to Alpatych with instructions to hand it to the Governor and return as quickly as possible if there was danger.

Having received all his orders, Alpatych put on a white beaver hat—a present from the prince—and carrying a stick as the prince did, went out accompanied by his family. Three well-fed roan horses stood harnessed to a small covered carriage.

The large bell was muffled and the small bells on the harness were stuffed with paper. The prince allowed no one at Bald Hills to drive with ringing bells, but on a long journey Alpatych liked to have them. His entourage—the senior clerk, a counting-house clerk, a scullery maid, a cook, two old women, a little page boy, the coachman, and various household servants—were seeing him off.

His daughter arranged chintz-covered down cushions for him to sit on and placed one behind his back. His old sister-in-law slipped in a small bundle, and one of the coachmen helped him into the carriage.
"There! There! Women's fussing! Women, women!" said Alpatych, puffing and speaking rapidly just as the prince did, and he climbed into the carriage.
After giving the clerk orders about the work to be done, Alpatych—no longer imitating the prince—lifted the hat from his bald head and crossed himself three times.
"If there's anything... come back, Yakov Alpatych! For Christ's sake, think of us!" cried his wife, referring to the rumors of war and the enemy.

"Women, women! Women's fussing!" muttered Alpatych to himself and set off on his journey, gazing at the fields of yellow rye and the still-green, thickly growing oats, and at other quite black fields just being plowed for the second time.

As he rode along, he looked with pleasure at the year's splendid crop of grain, studied the strips of rye already being harvested here and there, made his mental calculations about the sowing and the harvest, and checked whether he had forgotten any of the prince's orders.
Having fed the horses twice along the way, he arrived at the town toward evening on the fourth of August.

Alpatych kept meeting and passing baggage trains and troops on the road. As he approached Smolensk, he heard the sounds of distant gunfire, but these didn't impress him. What struck him most was the sight of a splendid field of oats in which a military camp had been pitched and which was being mowed down by the soldiers, obviously for fodder. This fact impressed Alpatych, but thinking about his own business he soon forgot it.

All the concerns of his life for more than thirty years had been bounded by the prince's will, and he never stepped beyond those limits. Anything not connected with carrying out the prince's orders didn't interest him and didn't even exist for Alpatych.

On reaching Smolensk on the evening of the fourth of August, he put up in the Gachina district across the Dnieper, at the inn kept by Ferapontov, where he had stayed for the last thirty years. Some thirty years ago, on Alpatych's advice, Ferapontov had bought a piece of forest from the prince, started trading, and now had a house, an inn, and a grain shop in the province. He was a stout, dark, red-faced peasant in his forties, with thick lips, a broad knob of a nose, similar knobs over his black frowning brows, and a round belly.
Wearing a waistcoat over his cotton shirt, Ferapontov was standing in front of his shop, which faced the street. Seeing Alpatych, he went up to him.
"You're welcome, Yakov Alpatych. Folks are leaving town, and you've come to it," said he.
"Why are they leaving town?" asked Alpatych.
"That's what I say. People are foolish! Always scared of the French."
"Women's fussing, women's fussing!" said Alpatych.
"Just what I think, Yakov Alpatych. What I say is: the orders are not to let them in, so that must be right. And the peasants are charging three rubles for carting—it's not Christian!"
Yakov Alpatych heard without really listening. He ordered a samovar and hay for his horses, and after having his tea, went to bed.

All night long troops were moving past the inn. The next morning Alpatych put on the jacket he wore only in town and went out on business. It was a sunny morning and by eight o'clock it was already hot. "A good day for harvesting," thought Alpatych.

From beyond the town, firing had been heard since early morning. By eight o'clock the boom of cannon was added to the sound of musket fire. Many people were hurrying through the streets and there were soldiers everywhere, but cabs were still driving about, shopkeepers stood at their doors, and church services were being held as usual. Alpatych went to the shops, to government offices, to the post office, and to the Governor's. In the offices and shops and at the post office, everyone was talking about the army and the enemy who was already attacking the town—everyone was asking what should be done, and all were trying to calm one another.

In front of the Governor's house, Alpatych found a large crowd of people, Cossacks, and one of the Governor's traveling carriages. At the entrance he met two local landowners, one of whom he knew. This man, a former captain of police, was saying angrily:

"It's no joke, you know! It's fine if you're single. 'One man ruined is just one man,' as the saying goes, but with thirteen in your family and all your property... They've brought us to utter ruin! What kind of governors are these? They should be hanged—the criminals!"
"Oh come, that's enough!" said the other.
"What do I care? Let him hear! We're not dogs," said the former police captain, and looking around, he noticed Alpatych.
"Oh, Yakov Alpatych! What brings you here?"

"To see the Governor, on his excellency's orders," answered Alpatych, lifting his chin and proudly thrusting his hand into the front of his coat as he always did when mentioning the prince. "He has ordered me to inquire into the state of affairs," he added.

"Yes, go and find out!" shouted the angry gentleman. "They've let things get to the point where there are no carts or anything!... There it is again, do you hear?" he said, pointing in the direction of the gunfire.
"They've brought us all to ruin... the criminals!" he repeated, and went down the steps.

Alpatych shook his head and went upstairs. In the waiting room were shopkeepers, women, and officials, all silently looking at one another. The door of the Governor's office opened and they all rose and pressed forward. An official ran out, said a few words to a merchant, called a stout official wearing a cross on his neck to follow him, and vanished again, clearly trying to avoid the inquiring looks and questions aimed at him. Alpatych stepped forward, and the next time the official emerged, he addressed him with one hand placed inside his buttoned coat, handing over two letters.
"To his Honor Baron Asch, from General-in-Chief Prince Bolkonsky," he announced with such solemnity and importance that the official turned to him and took the letters.
A few minutes later the Governor received Alpatych and hurriedly said:

"Inform the prince and princess that I knew nothing—I was acting on the highest instructions—here..." and he handed Alpatych a document. "Still, as the prince is unwell, my advice is that they should go to Moscow. I'm about to leave myself. Inform them..."
But the Governor didn't finish: a dusty, sweating officer ran into the room and began speaking rapidly in French. The Governor's face expressed terror.
"Go," he said, nodding to Alpatych, and began questioning the officer.

Anxious, frightened, helpless glances were turned on Alpatych when he came out of the Governor's office. Now involuntarily listening to the gunfire, which had drawn nearer and grown louder, Alpatych hurried back to his inn. The paper from the Governor said this:

"I assure you that the town of Smolensk is not in the slightest danger as yet and it is unlikely that it will be threatened. I from one side and Prince Bagration from the other are marching to unite our forces before Smolensk, which junction will be effected on the 22nd instant, and both armies with their united forces will defend our compatriots of the province entrusted to your care till our efforts shall have beaten back the enemies of our Fatherland, or till the last warrior in our valiant ranks has perished. From this you will see that you have every right to reassure the inhabitants of Smolensk, for those defended by two such brave armies may feel assured of victory." (Instructions from Barclay de Tolly to Baron Asch, the civil governor of Smolensk, 1812.)
People were anxiously roaming about the streets.

Carts piled high with household goods—chairs, cupboards—kept emerging from the yards and moving along the streets. Loaded carts stood at the house next to Ferapontov's, and women were wailing and weeping as they said goodbye. A small dog ran barking around in front of the harnessed horses.

Alpatych entered the inn yard at a quicker pace than usual and went straight to the shed where his horses and carriage were. The coachman was asleep. He woke him up, told him to harness the horses, and went into the building. From the innkeeper's room came the sounds of a child crying, the desperate sobs of a woman, and the hoarse, angry shouting of Ferapontov. The cook came running through the passage like a frightened hen, just as Alpatych entered.
"He's beaten her to death. Killed the mistress!... Beat her... dragged her around!"
"What for?" asked Alpatych.

"She kept begging to leave. She's a woman! 'Take me away,' she says, 'don't let me die with my little children! Everyone else has gone,' she says, 'so why don't we go?' And he started beating her and dragging her around!"
At these words Alpatych nodded as if in approval, and not wanting to hear more, went to the door of the room across from the innkeeper's, where he had left his purchases.
"You brute, you murderer!" screamed a thin, pale woman who, with a baby in her arms and her headscarf torn off, burst through the door at that moment and ran down the steps into the yard.
Ferapontov came out after her, but seeing Alpatych, he adjusted his waistcoat, smoothed his hair, yawned, and followed Alpatych into the opposite room.
"Leaving already?" he said.
Alpatych, without answering or looking at his host, sorted his packages and asked how much he owed.
"We'll settle up! Well, did you see the Governor?" asked Ferapontov. "What's been decided?"
Alpatych replied that the Governor hadn't told him anything definite.

"With our kind of business, how can we just leave?" said Ferapontov. "We'd have to pay seven rubles a cartload to Dorogobutz, and I tell them it's not Christian to charge that! Selivanov, now, he made a good deal last Thursday—sold flour to the army at nine rubles a sack. Will you have some tea?" he added.
While the horses were being harnessed, Alpatych and Ferapontov drank tea and talked about the price of grain, the crops, and the good weather for harvesting.

"Well, it seems to be getting quieter," remarked Ferapontov, finishing his third cup of tea and getting up. "Our boys must have gotten the upper hand. They had orders not to let them in. So we've got the strength, it seems... They say the other day Platov drove them into the river Marina and drowned some eighteen thousand in one day."

Alpatych collected his parcels, handed them to the coachman who had come in, and settled up with the innkeeper. The noise of wheels, hooves, and bells was heard from the gateway as his little carriage drove out.

It was by now late in the afternoon. Half the street was in shadow, the other half brightly lit by the sun. Alpatych looked out of the window and went to the door. Suddenly the strange sound of a far-off whistling and thud was heard, followed by a boom of cannon blending into a dull roar that set the windows rattling.

He went out into the street: two men were running past toward the bridge. From different directions came whistling sounds and the thud of cannon balls and bursting shells falling on the town. But these sounds were barely noticed compared to the noise of the firing outside the town and drew little attention from the inhabitants. The town was being bombarded by a hundred and thirty guns that Napoleon had ordered up after four o'clock. The people didn't immediately grasp the meaning of this bombardment.

At first the noise of falling bombs and shells only aroused curiosity. Ferapontov's wife, who until then had not stopped wailing under the shed, became quiet and, with the baby in her arms, went to the gate, listening to the sounds and gazing in silence at the people.

The cook and a shop assistant came to the gate. With lively curiosity everyone tried to catch a glimpse of the projectiles as they flew overhead. Several people came around the corner talking excitedly.
"What power!" remarked one. "Smashed the roof and ceiling to splinters!"
"Plowed up the ground like a pig," said another.
"That's the stuff—gets the blood going!" laughed the first. "Lucky you jumped aside, or it would have flattened you!"

Others joined them and stopped to tell how cannon balls had fallen on a house close by. Meanwhile still more projectiles—now with the swift, sinister whistle of a cannon ball, now with the agreeable intermittent whistle of a shell—flew over people's heads incessantly, but not one fell nearby; they all flew over. Alpatych was getting into his carriage. The innkeeper stood at the gate.
"What are you staring at?" he shouted at the cook, who in her red skirt with sleeves rolled up, bare elbows swinging, had stepped to the corner to listen to what was being said.
"What a sight!" she exclaimed, but hearing her master's voice, she turned back, pulling down her tucked-up skirt.
Once more something whistled, but this time much closer, swooping down like a little bird; a flame flashed in the middle of the street, something exploded, and the street was shrouded in smoke.
"Scoundrel, what are you doing?" shouted the innkeeper, rushing to the cook.

At that moment the pitiful wailing of women was heard from different directions, the frightened baby began to cry, and people crowded silently with pale faces around the cook. The loudest sound in that crowd was her wailing.
"Oh-h-h! Dear souls, dear kind souls! Don't let me die! My good souls!..."

Five minutes later no one remained in the street. The cook, with her thigh broken by a shell fragment, had been carried into the kitchen. Alpatych, his coachman, Ferapontov's wife and children, and the house porter were all sitting in the cellar, listening. The roar of guns, the whistling of projectiles, and the pitiful moaning of the cook—which rose above the other sounds—did not stop for a moment. The mistress rocked and hushed her baby and when anyone came into the cellar asked in a pathetic whisper what had become of her husband, who had stayed in the street. A shopman who entered told her that her husband had gone with others to the cathedral, from where they were fetching the miracle-working icon of Smolensk.

Toward dusk the cannonade began to die down. Alpatych left the cellar and stood in the doorway. The evening sky that had been so clear was clouded with smoke, through which, high up, the crescent of the new moon shone strangely. Now that the terrible din of the guns had ceased, a hush seemed to reign over the town, broken only by the rustle of footsteps, the moaning, the distant cries, and the crackling of fires that seemed to be everywhere. The cook's moans had now subsided. On two sides, black curling clouds of smoke rose and spread from the fires. Through the streets, soldiers in various uniforms walked or ran in all directions like ants from a ruined anthill. Several of them ran into Ferapontov's yard before Alpatych's eyes. Alpatych went out to the gate. A retreating regiment, crowding and hurrying, blocked the street.
Noticing him, an officer said: "The town is being abandoned. Get out, get out!" and then, turning to the soldiers, shouted:
"I'll teach you to run into people's yards!"

Alpatych went back inside, called the coachman, and told him to get moving. Ferapontov's whole household came out too, following Alpatych and the coachman. The women, who had been silent until then, suddenly began to wail as they looked at the fires—the smoke and even the flames of which could be seen in the fading twilight—and as if in answer, the same kind of wailing was heard from other parts of the street. Inside the shed, Alpatych and the coachman arranged the tangled reins and traces of their horses with trembling hands.

As Alpatych was driving out of the gate, he saw about ten soldiers in Ferapontov's open shop, talking loudly and filling their bags and packs with flour and sunflower seeds. Just then Ferapontov returned and entered his shop. Seeing the soldiers, he started to shout at them, but suddenly stopped and, clutching at his hair, burst into sobs and laughter:
"Take it all, boys! Don't let those devils get it!" he cried, grabbing some bags of flour himself and throwing them into the street.
Some of the soldiers were frightened and ran away; others went on filling their bags. Seeing Alpatych, Ferapontov turned to him:
"Russia is done for!" he cried. "Alpatych, I'll set the place on fire myself. We're done for!" and Ferapontov ran into the yard.

Soldiers were passing in a constant stream along the street, completely blocking it, so that Alpatych couldn't get out and had to wait. Ferapontov's wife and children were also sitting in a cart, waiting until they could drive out.

Night had come. There were stars in the sky and the new moon shone out through the smoke that screened it. On the sloping descent to the Dnieper, Alpatych's cart and the innkeeper's wife's cart, slowly moving among the rows of soldiers and other vehicles, had to stop. In a side street near the crossroads where the vehicles had stopped, a house and some shops were on fire. The fire was already burning itself out. The flames would die down and disappear in black smoke, then suddenly flare up again, lighting with strange clarity the faces of the people crowding at the crossroads. Dark figures moved about before the fire, and through the incessant crackling of the flames, talking and shouting could be heard. Seeing that his carriage couldn't move for some time, Alpatych got down and turned into the side street to look at the fire. Soldiers were constantly rushing back and forth, and he saw two of them and a man in a rough coat dragging burning beams into another yard across the street, while others carried bundles of hay.

Alpatych went up to a large crowd standing before a tall barn that was blazing fiercely. The walls were all on fire, the back wall had collapsed, the wooden roof was caving in, and the rafters were ablaze. The crowd was obviously watching for the roof to fall, and Alpatych watched for it too.
"Alpatych!" a familiar voice suddenly called out to the old man.
"Your excellency! Mercy on us!" answered Alpatych, immediately recognizing the voice of his young prince.
Prince Andrew, in his riding cloak and mounted on a black horse, was looking at Alpatych from the back of the crowd.
"Why are you here?" he asked.
"Your... your excellency," stammered Alpatych and broke into sobs. "Are we really lost? Master!..."
"Why are you here?" Prince Andrew repeated.
At that moment the flames flared up and illuminated his young master's pale, worn face. Alpatych told how he had been sent to Smolensk and how difficult it was to get away.
"Are we really completely lost, your excellency?" he asked again.
Prince Andrew, without answering, took out a notebook, raised his knee, and began writing in pencil on a page he tore out. He wrote to his sister:
"Smolensk is being abandoned. Bald Hills will be occupied by the enemy within a week. Leave immediately for Moscow. Let me know at once when you start. Send word by special messenger to Usvyazh."

Having written this and given the paper to Alpatych, he told him how to arrange for the departure of the prince, the princess, his son, and the boy's tutor, and how and where to let him know immediately. Before he had finished giving these instructions, a chief of staff followed by his suite galloped up to him.

"You are a colonel?" shouted the chief of staff in a voice with a German accent, familiar to Prince Andrew. "Houses are being set on fire in your presence and you just stand by! What does this mean? You will answer for it!" shouted Berg, who was now assistant to the chief of staff of the left flank of the first army's infantry—a position which, as Berg put it, was "very pleasant and well in view."
Prince Andrew looked at him and, without replying, went on speaking to Alpatych.
"So tell them that I will wait for a reply until the tenth, and if by the tenth I don't get word that they've all left, I'll have to drop everything and come to Bald Hills myself."
"Prince," said Berg, recognizing Prince Andrew, "I only spoke because I have to follow orders, because I always follow them exactly... You must please excuse me," he went on apologetically.
Something cracked in the flames. The fire died down for a moment and wreaths of black smoke rolled from under the roof. There was another terrible crash and something huge collapsed.

"Ou-rou-rou!" yelled the crowd, echoing the crash of the collapsing barn roof, from which the burning grain gave off a cake-like aroma all around. The flames flared up again, lighting the animated, delighted, exhausted faces of the spectators.
The man in the rough coat raised his arms and shouted:
"It's going great, boys! Now it's really blazing... Beautiful!"
"That's the owner himself," cried several voices.
"Well then," continued Prince Andrew to Alpatych, "tell them everything I've said"; and without a word to Berg, who stood mute beside him, he touched his horse and rode down the side street.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter V
paragraphs: From Smolensk the troops continued to retreat, with the enemy in pursuit. On the tenth of August the regiment Prince Andrew commanded was marching along the highway past the avenue leading to Bald Hills. Heat and drought had continued for more than three weeks. Each day fluffy clouds floated across the sky and occasionally veiled the sun, but toward evening the sky cleared again and the sun set in reddish-brown mist. Heavy night dews alone refreshed the earth. The unharvested grain was scorched and shedding its seeds. The marshes dried up. The cattle lowed from hunger, finding no food on the sun-parched meadows. Only at night and in the forests, while the dew lasted, was there any freshness. But on the road—the highway along which the troops marched—there was no freshness even at night or when the road passed through forest; the dew was imperceptible on the sandy dust churned up more than six inches deep. As soon as day dawned, the march began. The artillery and baggage wagons moved silently through the deep dust that rose to the very wheel hubs, and the infantry sank ankle-deep in that soft, choking, hot dust that never cooled even at night. Some of this dust was kneaded by feet and wheels, while the rest rose and hung like a cloud over the troops, settling in eyes, ears, hair, and nostrils, and worst of all in the lungs of men and animals as they moved along that road. The higher the sun rose, the higher rose that cloud of dust, and through the screen of its hot fine particles one could look with the naked eye at the sun, which showed like a huge crimson ball in the unclouded sky. There was no wind, and the men choked in that motionless air. They marched with handkerchiefs tied over their noses and mouths. When they passed through a village, they all rushed to the wells and fought for the water, drinking it down to the mud.

Prince Andrew was in command of a regiment, and the management of that regiment—the welfare of the men and the necessity of receiving and giving orders—absorbed him entirely. The burning of Smolensk and its abandonment marked an epoch in his life. A new feeling of anger against the enemy made him forget his own sorrow. He devoted himself entirely to the affairs of his regiment and was considerate and kind to his men and officers. In the regiment they called him "our prince," were proud of him, and loved him. But he was kind and gentle only to those of his regiment, to Timokhin and the like—people completely new to him, belonging to a different world, who could not know or understand his past. As soon as he encountered a former acquaintance or anyone from the staff, he bristled up at once and became spiteful, ironic, and contemptuous. Everything that reminded him of his past was repugnant to him, and so in his relations with that former world he confined himself to trying to do his duty and not be unfair.

In truth, everything presented itself in a dark and gloomy light to Prince Andrew, especially after the abandonment of Smolensk on the sixth of August (he believed it could and should have been defended) and after his sick father had been forced to flee to Moscow, leaving his beloved Bald Hills—which he had built and populated—to be plundered. But despite this, thanks to his regiment, Prince Andrew had something to think about that was entirely separate from general questions. Two days earlier he had received news that his father, son, and sister had left for Moscow; and though there was nothing for him to do at Bald Hills, Prince Andrew, with a characteristic desire to aggravate his own grief, decided he had to ride there.

He ordered his horse saddled and, leaving his regiment on the march, rode to his father's estate where he had been born and spent his childhood. Riding past the pond where there had always been dozens of women chattering as they rinsed their laundry or beat it with wooden paddles, Prince Andrew noticed there wasn't a soul about, and the little washing dock, torn from its place and half submerged, was floating on its side in the middle of the pond. He rode to the gatekeeper's lodge. No one was at the stone entrance gates of the drive and the door was open. Grass had already begun to grow on the garden paths, and horses and calves were wandering through the English park. Prince Andrew rode up to the greenhouse; some of the glass panes were broken, and some of the trees in tubs were overturned, others dried up. He called for Taras the gardener, but no one replied. Having gone around the corner of the greenhouse to the ornamental garden, he saw that the carved garden fence was broken and branches of the plum trees had been torn off with the fruit. An old peasant whom Prince Andrew had often seen at the gate in his childhood was sitting on a green garden seat, weaving a bast shoe.

He was deaf and didn't hear Prince Andrew ride up. He was sitting on the bench the old prince used to like to sit on, and beside him strips of bast were hanging on the broken and withered branch of a magnolia.

Prince Andrew rode up to the house. Several lime trees in the old garden had been cut down, and a piebald mare and her foal were wandering among the rosebushes in front of the house. The shutters were all closed except at one open window. A little servant boy, seeing Prince Andrew, ran into the house. Alpatych, having sent his family away, was alone at Bald Hills, sitting indoors reading the Lives of the Saints. On hearing that Prince Andrew had come, he went out with his spectacles on his nose, buttoning his coat, and hastily stepping up, without a word began weeping and kissing Prince Andrew's knee.

Then, vexed at his own weakness, he turned away and began reporting on the state of affairs. Everything precious and valuable had been moved to Bogucharovo. Seventy quarters of grain had also been carted away. The hay and the spring grain, of which Alpatych said there had been a remarkable crop that year, had been commandeered by the troops and mowed down while still green. The peasants were ruined; some had also gone to Bogucharovo, and only a few remained.
Without waiting to hear him finish, Prince Andrew asked:
"When did my father and sister leave?"—meaning when did they leave for Moscow.

Alpatych, understanding the question to be about their departure for Bogucharovo, replied that they had left on the seventh, and again went into details about the estate management, asking for instructions.
"Should I let the troops have the oats and take a receipt? We still have six hundred quarters left," he asked.

"What can I tell him?" thought Prince Andrew, looking down at the old man's bald head shining in the sun and seeing from his expression that the old man himself understood how out of place these questions were and only asked them to ease his grief.
"Yes, let them have it," replied Prince Andrew.

"If you noticed some disorder in the garden," said Alpatych, "it was impossible to prevent. Three regiments came through and spent the night—dragoons, mostly. I took down the name and rank of their commanding officer so I could file a complaint."
"Well, what are you going to do? Stay here if the enemy occupies the place?" asked Prince Andrew.
Alpatych turned his face to Prince Andrew, looked at him, and suddenly with a solemn gesture raised his arm.
"He is my refuge! His will be done!" he exclaimed.
A group of bareheaded peasants was approaching across the meadow toward the prince.
"Well, goodbye!" said Prince Andrew, bending down to Alpatych. "You must leave too—take away what you can, and tell the serfs to go to the Ryazan estate or to the one near Moscow."
Alpatych clung to Prince Andrew's leg and burst into sobs. Gently freeing himself, the prince spurred his horse and galloped down the avenue.

The old man was still sitting in the ornamental garden, like a fly sitting motionless on the face of a loved one who is dead, tapping the shoe last on which he was weaving the bast shoe, and two little girls, running out from the greenhouse carrying plums they had picked in their skirts, came upon Prince Andrew. Seeing the young master, the older one seized her younger companion by the hand with a frightened look and hid with her behind a birch tree, not stopping to pick up some green plums they had dropped.

Prince Andrew turned away with startled haste, unwilling to let them see they had been noticed. He felt sorry for the pretty frightened little girl, was afraid of looking at her, and yet felt an irresistible desire to do so. A new sensation of comfort and relief came over him when, seeing these girls, he realized that other human interests existed entirely apart from his own and just as legitimate as those that consumed him. These girls clearly wanted nothing more passionately than to carry away and eat those green plums without getting caught—and Prince Andrew shared their wish for the success of their enterprise. He couldn't resist looking at them once more. Believing the danger had passed, they sprang from their hiding place and, chirping something in their shrill little voices and holding up their skirts, scampered merrily and quickly on their bare, sunburned feet across the meadow grass.

Prince Andrew felt somewhat refreshed from having ridden off the dusty highway along which the troops were moving. But not far from Bald Hills he came back to the road and overtook his regiment at its halt by the dam of a small pond. It was past one o'clock. The sun, a red ball through the dust, burned and scorched his back unbearably through his black coat. The dust always hung motionless above the buzz of talk from the resting troops. There was no wind. As he crossed the dam, Prince Andrew caught the smell of ooze and freshness from the pond. He longed to get into that water, however dirty it might be, and he glanced at the pond from which came sounds of shrieks and laughter. The small, muddy, green pond had risen visibly more than a foot above the dam, because it was full of naked white bodies of soldiers with sunburned hands, necks, and faces, splashing about in it. All this naked white human flesh, laughing and shrieking, floundered about in that dirty pool like fish stuffed into a watering can, and the suggestion of merriment in that floundering mass made it all the more pitiful.

One fair-haired young soldier of the third company, whom Prince Andrew knew and who had a strap around the calf of one leg, crossed himself, stepped back to get a running start, and plunged into the water; another, a dark noncommissioned officer who was always shaggy, stood waist-deep in the water joyfully flexing his muscular figure and snorted with satisfaction as he poured water over his head with hands blackened to the wrists. There were sounds of men slapping one another, yelling, and spluttering.

Everywhere on the bank, on the dam, and in the pond, there was healthy, white, muscular flesh. The officer Timokhin, with his little red nose, standing on the dam drying himself with a towel, felt embarrassed at seeing the prince but made up his mind to address him anyway.
"It's really nice, your excellency! Wouldn't you like to?" he said.
"It's dirty," replied Prince Andrew, making a face.
"We'll clear it out for you in a minute," said Timokhin, and, still undressed, ran off to clear the men out of the pond.
"The prince wants to bathe."
"What prince? Ours?" said many voices, and the men were in such a hurry to clear out that the prince could barely stop them. He decided he would rather wash himself with water in the barn.

"Flesh, bodies, cannon fodder!" he thought, looking at his own naked body and shuddering—not from cold but from a feeling of disgust and horror he didn't fully understand, aroused by the sight of that immense number of bodies splashing in the dirty pond.
On the seventh of August, Prince Bagration wrote as follows from his quarters at Mikhailovka on the Smolensk road:
Dear Count Alexei Andreevich—(He was writing to Arakcheev but knew the letter would be read by the Emperor, so he weighed every word as carefully as he could.)

I expect the Minister (Barclay de Tolly) has already reported the abandonment of Smolensk to the enemy. It is pitiable and sad, and the whole army is in despair that this most important place has been needlessly abandoned. I, for my part, begged him personally and most urgently, and finally wrote to him, but nothing would persuade him. I swear to you on my honor that Napoleon was in a tighter spot than ever before and might have lost half his army but could not have taken Smolensk. Our troops fought, and are fighting, as never before. With fifteen thousand men I held the enemy at bay for thirty-five hours and beat him; but he would not hold out even for fourteen hours. It is a disgrace, a stain on our army, and as for him, it seems to me he should not go on living. If he reports that our losses were heavy, it is not true; perhaps about four thousand, not more, and not even that; but even were they ten thousand, that's war! But the enemy has lost far more...

What would it have cost him to hold out for another two days? They would have had to retreat on their own, for they had no water for men or horses. He gave me his word he would not retreat, but suddenly sent orders that he was pulling out that night. We cannot fight this way, or we'll soon bring the enemy right to Moscow...

There is a rumor that you are thinking of peace. God forbid that you should make peace after all our sacrifices and such insane retreats! You would turn all Russia against you, and every one of us would be ashamed to wear the uniform. If it has come to this—we must fight as long as Russia stands and as long as there are men able to fight...

One man ought to be in command, not two. Your Minister may perhaps be a good minister, but as a general he is not merely bad but execrable, yet the fate of our whole country has been entrusted to him... I am truly beside myself with frustration; forgive my writing bluntly. It is clear that whoever advocates making peace, and that the Minister should command the army, does not love our sovereign and desires the ruin of us all. So I write to you frankly: call up the militia. For the Minister is leading these visitors of ours straight to Moscow in the most masterly way. The whole army regards the Imperial aide-de-camp Wolzogen with the greatest suspicion. He is said to be more Napoleon's man than ours, and he is forever advising the Minister. I am not merely civil to him but obey him like a corporal, though I am his senior. This is painful, but loving my benefactor and sovereign, I submit. Only I am sorry for the Emperor, that he entrusts our fine army to such a man... Consider that on our retreat we have lost through exhaustion and left in hospitals more than fifteen thousand men, and had we attacked this would not have happened. Tell me, for God's sake, what will Russia—our mother Russia—say to our being so frightened? And why are we abandoning our good and brave Fatherland to such rabble, planting feelings of hatred and shame in all our people? What are we scared of and whom are we afraid of? It is not my fault that the Minister is indecisive, cowardly, dense, slow, and has every bad quality. The whole army weeps over it and curses him...

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: Among the countless categories that can be applied to the phenomena of human life, one may distinguish between those where substance matters most and those where form does. To the latter—as distinct from village, country, provincial, or even Moscow life—we may assign Petersburg life, and especially the life of its salons. That salon life is unchanging. Since 1805 we had made peace and quarreled again with Bonaparte and had made constitutions and unmade them, but the salons of Anna Pavlovna and Helene remained exactly as they had been—one seven and the other five years before. At Anna Pavlovna's they spoke with puzzlement of Bonaparte's successes, just as before, and saw in them and in the European sovereigns' submission to him a malicious conspiracy whose sole purpose was to cause unpleasantness and anxiety to the court circle that Anna Pavlovna represented. And in Helene's salon, which Rumyantsev himself honored with his visits, regarding Helene as a remarkably intelligent woman, they spoke with the same enthusiasm in 1812 as in 1808 of the "great nation" and the "great man" and regretted our rift with France, a rift which, according to them, ought to be promptly ended by peace.

Lately, since the Emperor's return from the army, there had been some excitement in these rival salon circles and some demonstrations of hostility between them, but each camp kept to its own line. In Anna Pavlovna's circle, only those Frenchmen who were dyed-in-the-wool royalists were admitted, and patriotic views were expressed: that one shouldn't attend the French theater and that maintaining the French troupe was costing the government as much as a whole army corps. The war's progress was eagerly followed, and only the most flattering reports about our army were circulated. In the French circle of Helene and Rumyantsev, reports of the enemy's cruelty and of the war were challenged, and all Napoleon's attempts at conciliation were discussed. In that circle they frowned on those who advised hurried preparations for moving the court and the girls' educational institutions under the Dowager Empress's patronage to Kazan. In Helene's circle, the war was regarded as a series of formal demonstrations that would very soon end in peace, and the view expressed by Bilibin—who was now quite at home in Helene's house, which every clever man was expected to visit—prevailed: that matters would be settled not by gunpowder but by those who invented it. In that circle, the Moscow enthusiasm (news of which had reached Petersburg along with the Emperor's return) was ridiculed sarcastically and very cleverly, though with great caution.

Anna Pavlovna's circle, on the contrary, was enraptured by this enthusiasm and spoke of it as Plutarch speaks of the deeds of the ancients. Prince Vasili, who still held his former important posts, formed a connecting link between the two circles. He visited his "good friend Anna Pavlovna" as well as his daughter's "diplomatic salon," and in his constant shuttling between the two camps often got confused, saying at Helene's what he should have said at Anna Pavlovna's, and vice versa.

Soon after the Emperor's return, Prince Vasili, in a conversation about the war at Anna Pavlovna's, severely criticized Barclay de Tolly but was undecided as to who ought to be appointed commander in chief. One of the visitors, usually referred to as "a man of great merit," having described how he had that day seen Kutuzov—the newly chosen chief of the Petersburg militia—presiding over the enrollment of recruits at the Treasury, cautiously suggested that Kutuzov might be the man to satisfy all requirements.
Anna Pavlovna remarked with a melancholy smile that Kutuzov had done nothing but cause the Emperor annoyance.

"I've talked and talked at the Assembly of the Nobility," Prince Vasili interrupted, "but they wouldn't listen to me. I told them his election as chief of the militia would not please the Emperor. They didn't listen."

"It's all this mania for opposition," he went on. "And for whom? It's all because we want to imitate the foolish enthusiasm of those Muscovites," Prince Vasili continued, forgetting for a moment that at Helene's one had to ridicule Moscow's enthusiasm, while at Anna Pavlovna's one had to be rapturous about it. But he corrected himself at once. "Now, is it fitting that Count Kutuzov, the oldest general in Russia, should preside at that tribunal? He'll get nothing for his trouble! How could they make a man commander in chief who can't mount a horse, who falls asleep in council, and has the very worst morals? A fine reputation he made at Bucharest! I don't speak of his capacity as a general, but at a time like this how can they appoint a decrepit, blind old man—positively blind? A fine idea, a blind general! He can't see a thing. Playing blindman's buff? He can't see at all!"
No one responded to his remarks.

This was perfectly correct on the twenty-fourth of July. But on the twenty-ninth of July, Kutuzov was given the title of Prince. This might indicate a wish to get rid of him, and so Prince Vasili's opinion remained valid, though he was in no hurry to repeat it. But on the eighth of August, a committee consisting of Field Marshal Saltykov, Arakcheev, Vyazmitinov, Lopukhin, and Kochubey met to consider the progress of the war. This committee concluded that our failures were due to a lack of unified command, and though its members were aware of the Emperor's dislike of Kutuzov, after brief deliberation they agreed to recommend his appointment as commander in chief. That same day Kutuzov was appointed commander in chief with full powers over the armies and over the entire region they occupied.

On the ninth of August, Prince Vasili met the "man of great merit" again at Anna Pavlovna's. The latter was very attentive to Anna Pavlovna because he wanted to be appointed director of one of the girls' educational institutions. Prince Vasili entered the room with the air of a happy conqueror who has achieved the object of his desires.

"Well, have you heard the great news? Prince Kutuzov is field marshal! All disagreements are over! I am so glad, so delighted! At last we have a real leader!" he said, glancing sternly and significantly around the drawing room.

The "man of great merit," despite his desire for the director's post, couldn't resist reminding Prince Vasili of his former opinion. Though this was impolite to Prince Vasili in Anna Pavlovna's drawing room, and also to Anna Pavlovna herself, who had received the news with delight, he couldn't resist the temptation.
"But, Prince, they say he's blind!" he said, echoing Prince Vasili's own words.
"Nonsense! He sees well enough," said Prince Vasili quickly, in a deep voice with a slight cough—the voice and cough he always used to dismiss difficulties.

"He sees well enough," he repeated. "And what I'm so pleased about is that our sovereign has given him full powers over all the armies and the whole region—powers no commander in chief has ever had before. He's a second autocrat," he concluded with a triumphant smile.
"God grant it! God grant it!" said Anna Pavlovna.
The "man of great merit," who was still a newcomer to court circles, wishing to flatter Anna Pavlovna by defending her earlier position on this question, observed:

"They say the Emperor was reluctant to give Kutuzov those powers. They say he blushed like a girl being read a romantic novel when he said to Kutuzov: 'Your Emperor and the Fatherland award you this honor.'"
"Perhaps the heart had no part in that speech," said Anna Pavlovna.

"Oh, no, no!" Prince Vasili warmly objected, now unwilling to yield Kutuzov to anyone; in his opinion Kutuzov was not only admirable but was adored by everybody. "No, that's impossible," he said, "for our sovereign valued him so highly before."
"God grant only that Prince Kutuzov assumes real power and doesn't let anyone put a spoke in his wheel," observed Anna Pavlovna.
Immediately understanding who she meant, Prince Vasili said in a whisper:
"I know for a fact that Kutuzov made it an absolute condition that the Tsarevich should not be with the army. Do you know what he said to the Emperor?"
And Prince Vasili repeated the words supposedly spoken by Kutuzov to the Emperor: "I can neither punish him if he does wrong nor reward him if he does right."
"Oh, a very wise man is Prince Kutuzov! I have known him a long time!"
"They even say," remarked the "man of great merit," who had not yet mastered courtly tact, "that his excellency made it an express condition that the sovereign himself should not be with the army."
As soon as he said this, both Prince Vasili and Anna Pavlovna turned away from him and glanced sadly at one another with a sigh at his naivety.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: While this was happening in Petersburg, the French had already passed Smolensk and were drawing ever closer to Moscow. Napoleon's historian Thiers, like his other historians, trying to justify his hero, says that Napoleon was drawn to the walls of Moscow against his will. He is as right as other historians who look for the explanation of historic events in the will of one man; he is as right as the Russian historians who maintain that Napoleon was drawn to Moscow by the skill of the Russian commanders. Here, besides the law of hindsight—which treats all the past as preparation for events that subsequently occur—the law of reciprocity comes in, confusing the whole matter. A good chess player who has lost a game is sincerely convinced his loss resulted from a mistake he made and looks for that mistake in the opening, forgetting that at every stage there were similar mistakes and that none of his moves were perfect. He only notices the mistake that catches his attention because his opponent took advantage of it. How much more complex than chess is the game of war, which occurs within limits of time, where it is not one will that moves lifeless objects, but everything results from countless conflicts of various wills!

After Smolensk, Napoleon sought a battle beyond Dorogobutz at Vyazma, and then at Tsarevo-Zaimishche, but it happened that due to a combination of innumerable circumstances, the Russians could not give battle until they reached Borodino, seventy miles from Moscow. From Vyazma, Napoleon ordered a direct advance on Moscow.

Moscow, the Asiatic capital of this great empire, the sacred city of Alexander's people, Moscow with its countless churches shaped like Chinese pagodas—this Moscow gave Napoleon's imagination no rest. On the march from Vyazma to Tsarevo-Zaimishche, he rode his light bay bobtailed horse accompanied by his Guards, his bodyguard, his pages, and his aides-de-camp. Berthier, his chief of staff, dropped behind to question a Russian prisoner captured by the cavalry. Followed by the interpreter Lelorgne d'Ideville, he overtook Napoleon at a gallop and reined in his horse with an amused expression.
* "Moscow, the Asiatic capital of this great empire, the sacred city of Alexander's people, Moscow with its countless churches shaped like Chinese pagodas."
"Well?" asked Napoleon.
"One of Platov's Cossacks says that Platov's corps is joining the main army and that Kutuzov has been appointed commander in chief. He's a very shrewd and talkative fellow."

Napoleon smiled and ordered them to give the Cossack a horse and bring the man to him. He wanted to talk to him personally. Several aides galloped off, and an hour later Lavrushka—the serf Denisov had handed over to Rostov—rode up to Napoleon in an orderly's jacket on a French cavalry saddle, with a cheerful, tipsy face. Napoleon told him to ride alongside and began questioning him.
"Are you a Cossack?"
"Yes, a Cossack, your Honor."

"The Cossack, not knowing in what company he was, for Napoleon's plain appearance had nothing about it that would reveal to an Eastern mind the presence of a monarch, talked with extreme familiarity about the incidents of the war," says Thiers, narrating this episode. In reality, Lavrushka had gotten drunk the day before and left his master without dinner, had been whipped, and was sent to the village to find chickens, where he went looting until the French took him prisoner. Lavrushka was one of those coarse, brazen lackeys who have seen all sorts of things, consider it essential to do everything in a mean and cunning way, are ready to perform any service for their master, and are sharp at guessing their master's baser impulses, especially those driven by vanity and pettiness.
Finding himself in Napoleon's company, whose identity he had easily and surely recognized, Lavrushka was not the least bit intimidated, and simply did his utmost to win his new master's favor.

He knew perfectly well that this was Napoleon, but Napoleon's presence could no more intimidate him than Rostov's, or a sergeant major with a rod, would have done—for he had nothing that either the sergeant major or Napoleon could take from him.

So he rattled on, telling all the gossip he had heard among the orderlies. Much of it was true. But when Napoleon asked whether the Russians thought they would beat Bonaparte or not, Lavrushka squinted and considered.
In this question he detected subtle cunning, as men of his type see cunning in everything, so he frowned and didn't answer right away.
"It's like this," he said thoughtfully. "If there's a battle soon, yours will win. That's right. But if three days pass, then after that, well, that same battle will drag on for a long time."

Lelorgne d'Ideville smilingly translated this to Napoleon as follows: "If a battle takes place within the next three days, the French will win, but if later, God knows what will happen." Napoleon didn't smile, though he was evidently in high good humor, and he ordered the words to be repeated.
Lavrushka noticed this and, to entertain him further, pretending not to know who Napoleon was, added:
"We know you've got Bonaparte and that he's beaten everybody in the world, but we're a different story..."—without knowing why or how this bit of boastful patriotism slipped out at the end.

The interpreter translated these words without the final phrase, and Bonaparte smiled. "The young Cossack made his mighty interlocutor smile," says Thiers. After riding a few paces in silence, Napoleon turned to Berthier and said he wanted to see how the news that he was talking to the Emperor himself—to that very Emperor who had inscribed his immortally victorious name on the Pyramids—would affect this child of the Don.
* "Child of the Don."
The fact was accordingly conveyed to Lavrushka.

Lavrushka, understanding that this was meant to confuse him and that Napoleon expected him to be frightened, promptly pretended to be astonished and awestruck to please his new masters—he opened his eyes wide and put on the expression he usually wore when being led off for a whipping. "As soon as Napoleon's interpreter had spoken," says Thiers, "the Cossack, seized by amazement, did not utter another word but rode on with his eyes fixed on the conqueror whose fame had reached him across the steppes of the East. All his talkativeness was suddenly arrested and replaced by a naive and silent feeling of admiration. Napoleon, after making the Cossack a present, had him set free like a bird restored to its native fields."

Napoleon rode on, dreaming of the Moscow that so captivated his imagination, and "the bird restored to its native fields" galloped back to our outposts, making up along the way all the things that hadn't happened but that he intended to tell his comrades. What had actually happened he didn't care to relate, because it didn't seem worth telling. He found the Cossacks, asked for the regiment operating with Platov's detachment, and by evening found his master Nicholas Rostov, quartered at Yankovo. Rostov was just mounting up for a ride around the neighboring villages with Ilyin; he gave Lavrushka another horse and took him along.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: Princess Mary was not in Moscow and out of danger, as Prince Andrew supposed.

After Alpatych's return from Smolensk, the old prince seemed suddenly to wake from a dream. He ordered the militiamen to be called up from the villages and armed, and wrote a letter to the commander in chief informing him that he had resolved to remain at Bald Hills to the last and defend it, leaving it to the commander in chief's discretion whether to take measures for Bald Hills' defense. He announced to his household that he would stay.

But while remaining himself, he ordered the departure of the princess and Dessalles with the little prince to Bogucharovo and then to Moscow. Princess Mary, alarmed by her father's feverish, sleepless activity after his previous apathy, could not bring herself to leave him alone and for the first time in her life dared to disobey him. She refused to go, and her father's fury crashed down on her like a terrible storm. He repeated every injustice he had ever done her. Trying to prove her guilty, he told her she had worn him out, had caused his quarrel with his son, had harbored nasty suspicions of him, and had made it her life's purpose to poison his existence. He drove her from his study, telling her that if she didn't leave it made no difference to him. He declared he did not wish to remember her existence and warned her not to dare let him see her. The fact that he did not, as she had feared, order her to be taken away by force, but only told her not to let him see her, cheered Princess Mary. She knew it proved that in the depth of his soul he was glad she was staying and had not left.

The morning after little Nicholas had departed, the old prince put on his full dress uniform and prepared to visit the commander in chief. His carriage was already at the door. Princess Mary saw him walk out of the house in his uniform with all his decorations and go down the garden to review his armed peasants and household servants. She sat by the window listening to his voice coming from the garden. Suddenly several men came running up the avenue with frightened faces.

Princess Mary ran out to the porch, down the flower-bordered path, and into the avenue. A large crowd of militiamen and servants were moving toward her, and in their midst several men were supporting by the arms and dragging along a little old man in a uniform and decorations. She ran up to him and, in the play of sunlight that fell in small round spots through the shade of the lime trees, could not be sure what change there was in his face. All she could see was that his former stern and determined expression had given way to one of timidity and helplessness. On seeing his daughter, he moved his helpless lips and made a hoarse sound. It was impossible to make out what he wanted. He was lifted up, carried to his study, and laid on the very couch he had so dreaded lately.
The doctor, who was fetched that same night, bled him and said the prince had had a stroke paralyzing his right side.
It was becoming more and more dangerous to remain at Bald Hills, and the next day they moved the prince to Bogucharovo, the doctor accompanying him.
By the time they reached Bogucharovo, Dessalles and the little prince had already left for Moscow.

For three weeks the old prince lay stricken with paralysis in the new house Prince Andrew had built at Bogucharovo, always in the same condition, getting neither better nor worse. He was unconscious and lay like a distorted corpse. He muttered unceasingly, his eyebrows and lips twitching, and it was impossible to tell whether he understood what was going on around him or not. One thing was certain—he was suffering and wanted to say something. But what it was, no one could tell: it might be some whim of a sick, half-mad old man, or it might relate to public affairs, or possibly to family concerns.

The doctor said this restlessness was meaningless and due to physical causes; but Princess Mary believed he was trying to tell her something, and the fact that her presence always increased his agitation confirmed her belief.

He was clearly suffering both physically and mentally. There was no hope of recovery. It was impossible for him to travel, and it would not do to let him die on the road. "Would it not be better if the end came—the very end?" Princess Mary sometimes thought. Night and day, barely sleeping at all, she watched him and, terrible to say, often watched him not hoping to find signs of improvement but wishing to spot symptoms that the end was approaching.

Strange as it was for her to admit this feeling, it was there. And what seemed still more terrible was that since her father's illness began (perhaps even earlier, when she stayed with him expecting something to happen), all the personal desires and hopes that had been forgotten or dormant within her had awakened. Thoughts that hadn't entered her mind for years—thoughts of a life free from the fear of her father, and even the possibility of love and family happiness—floated continually through her imagination like temptations of the devil. Push them aside as she might, questions kept recurring about how she would arrange her life now, after this. These were temptations of the devil, and Princess Mary knew it. She knew that the only weapon against him was prayer, and she tried to pray. She assumed the posture of prayer, looked at the icons, repeated the words of a prayer, but she could not pray. She felt that a different world had taken hold of her—a world of strenuous and free activity, entirely opposed to the spiritual world in which she had previously been confined and in which her greatest comfort had been prayer. She could not pray, could not weep, and worldly cares possessed her.
It was becoming dangerous to stay at Bogucharovo. News of the French approach came from all sides, and in one village ten miles from Bogucharovo, a homestead had been looted by French marauders.

The doctor insisted on the necessity of moving the prince; the provincial Marshal of the Nobility sent an official to Princess Mary to urge her to get away as quickly as possible; and the police chief, having come to Bogucharovo, urged the same thing, saying the French were only about twenty-five miles away, that French proclamations were circulating in the villages, and that if the princess did not take her father away before the fifteenth, he could not answer for the consequences.

The princess decided to leave on the fifteenth. The cares of preparation and giving orders, for which everyone came to her, occupied her all day. She spent the night of the fourteenth as usual, without undressing, in the room next to the one where the prince lay. Several times, waking up, she heard his groans and muttering, the creaking of his bed, and the steps of Tikhon and the doctor as they turned him over. Several times she listened at the door, and it seemed to her that his muttering was louder than usual and that they were turning him more often. She could not sleep, and several times went to the door and listened, wanting to go in but unable to decide. Though he didn't speak, Princess Mary saw and knew how unwelcome every sign of worry on his account was to him. She had noticed how he turned away from the look she sometimes fixed on him involuntarily. She knew that going in during the night at an unusual hour would irritate him.

But never had she felt so sad for him or so afraid of losing him. She recalled her entire life with him, and in every word and act found an expression of his love for her. Occasionally, among these memories, temptations of the devil would surge into her imagination: thoughts of how things would be after his death, and how her new, free life would be arranged. But she drove these thoughts away with disgust. Toward morning he became quiet and she fell asleep.

She woke late. The honesty that often comes with waking showed her clearly what mattered most about her father's illness. On waking, she listened to what was happening behind the door and, hearing him groan, said to herself with a sigh that things were still the same.
"But what could have happened? What did I want? I want his death!" she cried with self-loathing.
She washed, dressed, said her prayers, and went out to the porch. Carriages without horses stood in front of it; things were being packed into the vehicles.

It was a warm, gray morning. Princess Mary stopped at the porch, still horrified by her own spiritual baseness, trying to collect her thoughts before going in to her father. The doctor came downstairs and came out to her.
"He's a little better today," he said. "I was looking for you. You can make out something of what he's saying. His head is clearer. Come in—he's asking for you..."

Princess Mary's heart beat so hard at this news that she turned pale and leaned against the wall to keep from falling. To see him, talk to him, to feel his eyes on her now that her whole soul was overflowing with those terrible, wicked temptations, was a torment of joy and terror.
"Come," said the doctor.

Princess Mary entered her father's room and went to his bed. He was lying on his back, propped up high, and his small bony hands with their knotted purple veins lay on the quilt; his left eye gazed straight ahead, his right eye was askew, and his brows and lips were motionless. He seemed altogether so thin, small, and pitiful. His face seemed to have shriveled or melted; his features had grown smaller. Princess Mary went up and kissed his hand. His left hand pressed hers so tightly that she understood he had been waiting for her for a long time. He twitched her hand, and his brows and lips quivered angrily.

She looked at him in dismay, trying to guess what he wanted. When she shifted position so that his left eye could see her face, he calmed down, not taking his eyes off her for several seconds. Then his lips and tongue moved, sounds came, and he began to speak, gazing timidly and imploringly at her, obviously afraid she might not understand.

Straining every faculty, Princess Mary looked at him. The clumsy efforts with which he moved his tongue made her lower her eyes and struggle to hold back the sobs rising in her throat. He said something, repeating the same words several times. She couldn't understand them, but tried to guess and repeated back what she thought he was saying.
"Mmm... ar... ate... ate..." he repeated several times.
It was quite impossible to understand these sounds. The doctor thought he had guessed, and asked: "Mary, are you afraid?" The prince shook his head, and repeated the same sounds again.
"My mind, my mind aches?" asked Princess Mary.
He made a mumbling sound in confirmation, took her hand, and began pressing it to different parts of his chest as if trying to find the right place for it.
"Always thoughts... about you... thoughts..." he then said, much more clearly than before, now that he was sure of being understood.
Princess Mary pressed her head against his hand, trying to hide her sobs and tears.
He moved his hand over her hair.
"I have been calling you all night..." he managed to say.
"If only I had known..." she said through her tears. "I was afraid to come in."
He pressed her hand.
"Weren't you sleeping?"
"No, I didn't sleep," said Princess Mary, shaking her head.
Unconsciously imitating her father, she now tried to express herself as he did—as much as possible by gestures—and her tongue too seemed to move with difficulty.

"Dear one... dearest..." Princess Mary couldn't quite make out what he had said, but from his look it was clear he had spoken a tender, loving word such as he had never used with her before. "Why didn't you come in?"
"And I was wishing for his death!" thought Princess Mary.
He was silent for a while.

"Thank you... daughter dear... for everything, for everything... forgive... thank you!... forgive!... thank you!" and tears began to flow from his eyes. "Call Andrew!" he said suddenly, and a childish, timid expression of doubt showed on his face.
He seemed to know himself that his request was meaningless. So at least it seemed to Princess Mary.
"I have a letter from him," she replied.
He looked at her with timid surprise.
"Where is he?"
"He's with the army, Father, at Smolensk."
He closed his eyes and was silent for a long time. Then, as if in answer to his own doubts and to confirm that he now understood and remembered everything, he nodded and reopened his eyes.
"Yes," he said softly and distinctly. "Russia is ruined. They've destroyed her."
And he began to sob, and tears again flowed from his eyes. Princess Mary could no longer hold back and wept as she gazed at his face.
He closed his eyes again. His sobs ceased. He pointed to his eyes, and Tikhon, understanding him, wiped away the tears.

Then he opened his eyes again and said something that none of them could understand for a long time, until at last Tikhon grasped it and repeated it. Princess Mary had been searching for the meaning of his words in the mood of what he had just been saying. She thought he was speaking of Russia, or Prince Andrew, of herself, of his grandson, or of his own death, and so she couldn't guess.
"Put on your white dress. I like it," was what he said.

Having understood this, Princess Mary sobbed even harder, and the doctor, taking her arm, led her out to the veranda, trying to soothe her and persuade her to prepare for the journey. After she had left the room, the prince began speaking again about his son, about the war, about the Emperor, angrily twitching his brows and raising his hoarse voice, and then he had a second and final stroke.

Princess Mary stayed on the veranda. The day had cleared; it was hot and sunny. She could understand nothing, think of nothing, feel nothing except passionate love for her father—a love such as she thought she had never felt until that moment. She ran out sobbing into the garden and as far as the pond, along the avenue of young lime trees Prince Andrew had planted.

"Yes... I... I... I wished for his death! Yes, I wanted it to end sooner... I wanted peace... And what will become of me? What use will peace be when he is gone?" Princess Mary murmured, pacing the garden with hurried steps and pressing her hands to her heaving chest.

When she had walked around the whole garden and come back to the house, she saw Mademoiselle Bourienne—who had remained at Bogucharovo and did not wish to leave—coming toward her with a stranger. This was the Marshal of the Nobility for the district, who had come in person to impress upon the princess the urgency of leaving immediately. Princess Mary listened without understanding him; she led him into the house, offered him lunch, and sat down with him. Then, excusing herself, she went to the door of the old prince's room. The doctor came out with an agitated face and said she couldn't go in.
"Go away, Princess! Go away... go away!"

She went back to the garden and sat down on the grass at the foot of the slope by the pond, where no one could see her. She didn't know how long she had been there when she was roused by the sound of a woman's footsteps hurrying along the path. She looked up. It was Dunyasha, her maid, who had obviously been looking for her and stopped short in alarm on seeing her mistress.
"Please come, Princess... The Prince," said Dunyasha in a breaking voice.
"Right away, I'm coming, I'm coming!" replied the princess hurriedly, not giving Dunyasha time to finish, and trying not to look at the girl, she ran toward the house.
"Princess, it is God's will! You must be prepared for everything," said the Marshal, meeting her at the door.
"Leave me alone; it's not true!" she cried angrily.

The doctor tried to stop her. She pushed him aside and ran to her father's door. "Why are these people with frightened faces blocking my way? I don't need any of them! And what are they doing here?" she thought. She opened the door and the bright daylight in that previously darkened room startled her. In the room were her nurse and other women. They all drew back from the bed, making way for her. He was still lying on the bed as before, but the stern expression on his quiet face made Princess Mary stop short at the threshold.

"No, he's not dead—it's impossible!" she told herself, and approached him, and suppressing the terror that gripped her, she pressed her lips to his cheek. But she stepped back at once. All the force of the tenderness she had been feeling for him vanished instantly, replaced by a feeling of horror at what lay before her. "No, he is no more! He is gone, but here where he was is something unfamiliar and hostile, some dreadful, terrifying, repulsive mystery!" And hiding her face in her hands, Princess Mary collapsed into the arms of the doctor, who caught her.

In the presence of Tikhon and the doctor, the women washed what had been the prince, bound up his head with a cloth so the mouth would not stiffen open, and with another cloth tied together the legs that were already spreading apart. Then they dressed him in his uniform with his decorations and placed his shriveled little body on a table. Heaven only knows who arranged all this and when, but it all seemed to happen by itself. Toward evening candles were burning around his coffin, a pall was spread over it, the floor was strewn with sprays of juniper, a printed prayer band was tucked under his shriveled head, and in a corner of the room a chanter sat reading the psalms.

Just as horses shy and snort and crowd around a dead horse, so the members of the household and strangers crowded into the drawing room around the coffin—the Marshal, the village Elder, peasant women—and all with fixed and frightened eyes, crossing themselves, bowed and kissed the old prince's cold and stiffened hand.
